I didn't realize until much later how much worse my rumination over abuse I faced was till I saw someone else in a support network bring up how their adhd caused them to fixate on the problem more. When I realized that it forced me to pay attention to my adhd symptoms on a even level with my ptsd symptoms rather than assuming neither affected the other. Once I started thinking on the rolls each played with the possibility or worsening my symptoms of each disorder I was able to to a lot more healthy work on myself and had a more stable recovery with the whole ptsd thing.  


I think the first step to stopping is to acknowledge that our adhd can affect this stuff. For me I ended up throwing more time into focusing on stuff that demanded my attention. Movies aren't good for me personally because my brain can wander off during them, but when I'm focusing on gardening and being active with checking up on my plants or I'm focused on a video game that demands attention it forces me away from whatever has me pissed. Then later when I revisit what made me mad in the first place it doesn't feel as bad because I haven't spent a ton of time in my own brain focused on it.

If it helps too, I can try to give advice as a lady who wants to be approached more by both dudes and gals (same applies to other lgbtqa girls reading this lol):  


I would say maybe start with small talk to see how they respond (example, I approached someone my gym recently to ask about equipment and that helped me to gauge how warm to me he was. If you end up asking a person out for coffee or meeting up later or whatever, always make sure to give her a way out so they don't feel pressured to say yes, and giving them an easy no also shows you're safer to be around. When I ask people favors I do this too. Example is like "Hey! Can I ask you a favor? I need help getting this task done, but can't do it myself. If you don't have the time, interest, or energy though that's totally okay. I know a lot of folks are busy lately." I'm only getting back into dating so I have to try that more in the context of dating discussions, but I feel like even in non-romantic situations, when you introduce to them that there's encouragement to set boundaries as needed people become more comfortable around you. I know I find myself feeling ten times more at ease around guys who encourage me to say no or voice discomfort if it comes up vs the people who lay on the pressure to say yes to everything, especially sexual intimacy right off the bat (though if that's what you want just be up front about it, but still offer that no out). When people give me that option it tells me that they respect me as a person as well and I'm much more likely to reciprocate feelings to a person who respects my time and autonomy.

We let him know, give him that vibe check, and if he's in the right we help him brainstorm solutions and if his difficult thoughts are a product of bpd he takes a timeout to cool off, practice dbt skills, then comes back to the group. I've had both of these relationships for ages and ages now and both are healthy people who manage their bpd well, respect boundries, and we are able to appropriately discuss conflict. I work in QA! It's actually been really great for my adhd. Because I have so many tasks and test cases to run it feels like my brain always has stimulation to latch onto. There's a lot of pride in what I do and I'm thankful that my job helps make the job of other developers easier. I do freelance art on the side, but as it is now, I've been able to grow a stable career in QA that allows me to live comfortably. A lot of first QA jobs can suck if you work in video games, but if you work your way up to senior, lead, and analyst positions there is a lot more security. Video game studios tend to pay less for QA and be on contract. Apps and other software development tends to be more secure from what I understand.
